"""
Cross-platform User and Credential domain model.

A first-class internal abstraction over the per-platform credential
vocabularies (the Z-Wave User Credential Command Class and the Matter
DoorLock cluster). The model is shaped so the current one-managed-slot to
one-user to one-Personal-Identification-Number-credential projection is a
thin pure function, while a future "user is the unit, multiple credentials"
world only needs to append to ``User.credentials`` -- no field changes.

These are pure value types with no Home Assistant dependencies. The credential
and capability types are immutable; ``User`` is a mutable aggregate of immutable
credentials. They do not change ``SlotCredential``, which remains the
coordinator's currency.
"""

async def set_lock_user(
    matter_client: MatterClient,
    node: MatterNode,
    *,
    user_index: int | None = None,
    user_name: str | None = None,
    user_unique_id: int | None = None,
    user_status: str | None = None,
    user_type: str | None = None,
    credential_rule: str | None = None,
) -> SetLockUserResult:
    """Add or update a user on the lock.

    When user_status, user_type, or credential_rule is None, defaults are used
    for new users and existing values are preserved for modifications.

    Returns typed dict with user_index on success.
    Raises HomeAssistantError on failure.
    """
    lock_endpoint = _get_lock_endpoint_or_raise(node)
    _ensure_usr_support(lock_endpoint)

    if user_index is None:
        # Adding new user - find first available slot
        max_users = (
            lock_endpoint.get_attribute_value(
                None, clusters.DoorLock.Attributes.NumberOfTotalUsersSupported
            )
            or 0
        )

        for idx in range(1, max_users + 1):
            get_user_response = await matter_client.send_device_command(
                node_id=node.node_id,
                endpoint_id=lock_endpoint.endpoint_id,
                command=clusters.DoorLock.Commands.GetUser(userIndex=idx),
            )
            if _get_attr(get_user_response, "userStatus") is None:
                user_index = idx
                break

        if user_index is None:
            raise NoAvailableUserSlotsError("No available user slots on the lock")

        user_status_enum = (
            USER_STATUS_REVERSE_MAP.get(
                user_status,
                clusters.DoorLock.Enums.UserStatusEnum.kOccupiedEnabled,
            )
            if user_status is not None
            else clusters.DoorLock.Enums.UserStatusEnum.kOccupiedEnabled
        )

        await matter_client.send_device_command(
            node_id=node.node_id,
            endpoint_id=lock_endpoint.endpoint_id,
            command=clusters.DoorLock.Commands.SetUser(
                operationType=clusters.DoorLock.Enums.DataOperationTypeEnum.kAdd,
                userIndex=user_index,
                userName=user_name,
                userUniqueID=user_unique_id,
                userStatus=user_status_enum,
                userType=USER_TYPE_REVERSE_MAP.get(
                    user_type,
                    clusters.DoorLock.Enums.UserTypeEnum.kUnrestrictedUser,
                )
                if user_type is not None
                else clusters.DoorLock.Enums.UserTypeEnum.kUnrestrictedUser,
                credentialRule=CRED

95	def _is_transient_credential_status(status: str) -> bool:
96	    """
97	    Return True for a SetCredential status that should be retried, not rejected.
98	
99	    HA's matter ``lock_helpers.set_lock_credential`` maps recognized DlStatus
100	    values to names (``success`` / ``failure`` / ``duplicate`` / ``occupied``)
101	    and formats anything else as ``unknown(<code>)`` --
102	    ``SET_CREDENTIAL_STATUS_MAP.get(status_code, f"unknown({status_code})")`` --
103	    discarding the raw code. So ``unknown(`` is the only signal LCM has for "the
104	    lock returned a status the helper did not recognize", and an unmapped status
105	    is treated as transient (route to the retry path) -- notably ``unknown(133)``
106	    observed while a lock is not fully ready right after startup (issue #1257) --
107	    rather than a definitive rejection that permanently disables the slot.
108	
109	    FRAGILE COUPLING: this depends on HA's private ``unknown(<code>)`` format,
110	    which has no stability contract. If that helper ever changes the format or
111	    starts mapping a code we rely on (e.g. 133 -> a real name), this predicate
112	    silently returns False and the #1257 not-ready case regresses to a permanent
113	    suspend. ``tests/providers/matter/test_provider.py`` pins the current format.
114	    """
115	    return status.startswith("unknown(")

content.text:
One fix is committed. The second was falsified by your own test suite, which changes what I can deliver.

## Shipped: `8b91cc36` on `fix/1538-matter-multilock`

The false in-sync, time-bounded via `PENDING_WRITE_TTL` (moved to `const.py` so the seam and the sync layer share one answer about one write). Full suite green — 2347 passed, coverage gate held, `prek` clean on the five changed files.

Mutation-tested rather than trusted to coverage:

| Mutant | Result |
|---|---|
| Drop the TTL guard (the original bug) | killed |
| Invert the comparison | killed |
| Never arm the deadline on a set | killed *(survived first pass — needed a new test)* |
| Arm the deadline in the past | killed |
| Expire the unreadable branch too | killed |
| `<=` instead of `<` | survives — one instant of a monotonic clock, no invariant to reach |

The "never arm the deadline" survivor is the one worth noting: nothing in the suite asserted that a set arms the window. Had that line been wrong, Schlage would have flapped out-of-sync through its entire cloud lag and rewritten the code every tick. I added `test_a_set_arms_the_window_it_will_be_trusted_in`, asserting through the in-sync decision rather than the attribute.

I also added an explicit guard that the *unreadable* branch never expires — expiring it would put every Matter slot permanently out of sync and rewrite it on a loop, which was the live hazard in this change.

## Reverted: the name-fallback fix

I restricted the cascade fall-through to `(InvalidArguments, InvalidCommand)` and your existing tests killed it immediately. The reason is worth keeping:

```python
UnknownError("InteractionModelError: InvalidCommand (0x85)")   # error_code=0
```

A Matter device-side rejection arrives as the **catch-all** `UnknownError`, with the IM status only in the message string. The typed `InvalidCommand` (`error_code=9`) is a matter-*server API* error — an entirely different namespace. So there is no exception type that separates "the lock refused this name" from "the lock was busy." Both are `UnknownError`.

`test_set_user_update_tolerates_matter_sdk_error` already encoded this, sourced from a production regression. My hierarchy-based reasoning looked airtight and was wrong about the one thing that mattered.

That leaves two honest options, and I don't think I should pick:

- **Parse the IM status from the message.** Precedent exists — `_is_transient_credential_status` greps for `unknown(` with a FRAGILE COUPLING comment. But I have no ground truth on what string a *busy* Aqara produces, so I'd be guessing at the discriminator, which is the thing I'd be relying on.
- **Stop classifying; make the degradation self-healing.** `async_set_user` already retries the canonical name first on every write, so a degraded name repairs itself the moment anything writes again. Nothing triggers that write, because the slot is in sync. Treating "the lock-side name isn't the canonical one" as work to do fixes it regardless of *why* the fallback fired.

I lean toward the second — it needs no unstable string and no ground truth I don't have — but it's a wider behavioral change than you scoped, so it's your call.

## For the issue comment

Two things worth telling the reporter, one of which corrects the brief:

**The attribution symptom is a write bug, not a resolver bug.** Every name in their table parses to the right slot, so the resolver reporting "slot 3" means the lock matched User D's PIN against slot 3's *stored credential*. Combined with User C's PIN opening nothing, that says a PIN landed against the wrong user at write time. Their hypothesis #9 (event attribution) is the wrong half; #7 (`SetUser`/`SetCredential` disagreement) is the right one.

**For the cross-lock deletion I need their debug log.** Four theories are dead by reproduction — the `pairs_removed` diff, the options flow, `reconcile` renumbering, and Matter node resolution. The only automatic user-deletion paths that exist are the `pairs_removed` loop and the `_set_credential` rollback, and neither fires against the retained lock. Given they were deleting users via Manage access in the same period, it's plausible Lock A was emptied by something else and the false in-sync — now fixed — is what made it look causal by preventing any repair. `lock_code_manager` debug logs spanning the removal would settle it.

Want me to open the PR and post that comment, and which way on the name fallback?

gh issue comment 1538 --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Thank you for this report — the sanitized `get_lock_users` dump and the physical PIN test table are what made most of the analysis below possible.

Four symptoms, so here is where each one stands.

### 2. False in-sync — root cause found, fix open as #1539

You were right that LCM was trusting its own state rather than verifying the credential. The specific mechanism: when a lock reports an active slot as **empty**, the in-sync check overrides that answer if the last PIN LCM wrote there still matches the configured one. That override exists for locks whose reads trail their writes, and its own comment describes it as trusting a *recent* set — but nothing made it recent. The value it compares against is written on every successful set and cleared only by a clear or a Home Assistant restart, so the override stood indefinitely.

So a credential you deleted through **Manage access** read as synchronized forever, and — because a slot in sync is a slot with nothing to do — never got a tick to put it back. That also explains the blank PIN sensors sitting next to `on` in-sync sensors.

#1539 gives that trust a deadline.

This one is very likely the reason the other symptoms looked worse than they were: whatever emptied Lock A, this is why LCM never noticed or repaired it.

### 4. `lcm3` / `lcm4` / `lcm5` — root cause found, fix in progress

Confirmed. LCM writes the Matter `userName` as `lcm:<slot>:<name>`, with fallbacks to `lcm<slot>` and then `<slot>` for firmware that rejects the colons. The bug is that it falls back on **any** error from the lock — including a transient one. Your logs show repeated poll failures, so a lock that was merely busy for a moment cost those slots their display name permanently, on a lock that demonstrably accepts colons (slots 1 and 2 prove it).

Worth stressing: `lcm3` still identifies the slot correctly. Nothing is mis-bound — only the display name was lost.

### 9 / 3. Attribution — this is a write bug, not an event bug

Your hypothesis #9 asks whether LCM mishandles a reported credential index that differs from its user index. I traced it, and the resolver is not where this goes wrong. Every name in your table decodes to the correct slot:

```
'lcm:1:User A' -> slot 1      'lcm3' -> slot 3
'lcm:2:User B' -> slot 2      'lcm4' -> slot 4
```

The slot bindings on the lock are intact, and the event resolver would map them correctly by either route it uses (`userIndex`, or the `credentialIndex` walk). So when User D's PIN produced a slot-3 event, the lock genuinely matched that PIN against **slot 3's stored credential**. Together with User C's PIN not opening the door at all, that points at a PIN landing against the wrong user at write time — your hypothesis **#7**, not #9.

The user_index ordering you saw (LCM slot 1 landing at Matter index 5) is benign, by the way — that is a failed first attempt for slot 1 being rolled back, freeing index 1 for slot 2, with slot 1 retrying into 5 later.

### 1. Cross-lock deletion — not reproduced, and I could use your logs

This is the one I have least to offer on, so rather than speculate, here is what I ruled out. I drove the real configuration paths with two locks and five users and watched every call:

- The removal diff is correct — removing lock B releases only lock B's slots. Lock A was told to release nothing.
- The options flow does not renumber anyone; existing users keep their slot numbers by design.
- The Matter provider resolves its node per device, so it cannot address the wrong lock.
- The only two code paths in the integration that can automatically delete a Matter user are the removal loop and a rollback of a just-created user. Neither can target a lock that stayed in the configuration.

Given you were also deleting users through **Manage access** during this period, one real possibility is that Lock A was emptied by something other than the removal, and the false in-sync above is what made it look causal — by guaranteeing nothing ever repaired it.

To get further I would need `lock_code_manager` debug logs covering the removal:

```yaml
logger:
  logs:
    custom_components.lock_code_manager: debug
```

The lines that would settle it name the lock and slot directly, e.g. `no LCM-owned user to release for slot N` or `Setting usercode on lock.<entity> slot N`. If those name Lock A during a removal of Lock B, that is the smoking gun and I will have it immediately.

### On your workaround

Your advice stands, and I would keep following it until #1539 ships: verify with `matter.get_lock_users` rather than the in-sync sensors, and hold off on using `code_slot_name` for security-sensitive attribution. Both cautions are well founded.
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

        2. **Legacy adoption** -- an *untagged* user owning a PIN

           LCM pinned ``credential_index`` to the LCM slot, so an
           untagged user owning a PIN at that index is almost certainly

           ``set_lock_user`` rewrites the name to the tagged form, and

input.command:
git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
fix: a lock holding a canonical name is not rejecting one for its charset

The Matter userName cascade writes lcm:<slot>:<name>, then lcm<slot>, then
the bare slot number, descending each time the lock refuses. It exists for
firmware that restricts userName to alphanumerics. It fired on any refusal.

Nothing in the exception says which refusal it was. A charset constraint
and a lock that was busy for a moment both arrive as the same catch-all
MatterError, carrying an interaction-model status in a message string with
no stability contract. Classifying on that was the first thing tried, and
the existing tests for this cascade were what showed it could not work.

So ask the lock instead. If it is holding a canonical name for some other
slot right now, it accepts the colons, and whatever it just refused was
not about them. Descending there trades a display name away for nothing.
Retry the canonical name instead, and let the moment pass.

That is issue #1538: on a lock storing lcm:1:User A and lcm:2:User B,
three further slots were written lcm3, lcm4 and lcm5 during a spell of
poll failures. The compact form still binds its slot -- nothing was
mis-identified -- and the next successful write to any of those slots
restores the display, since the cascade always starts from the canonical
name. But nothing writes to a slot that is already in sync, so what a
moment cost stayed on the lock. There is a test for that recovery too:
it is what lets this change only have to prevent the degradation rather
than also undo it.

Only the canonical format counts as proof. parse_tag also recognizes the
compact and slot-only forms, and accepting those would take the cascade's
own output as evidence that the cascade was unnecessary.

async_set_user now reads the user list once and answers both questions
from it -- which user anchors the slot, and whether colons are proven --
rather than paying a second round trip on a link already timing out.
MSG
git push -q origin fix/1538-matter-multilock && git log --oneline -2

Two independent root causes from #1538, each with its own commit.

## 1. A lock reporting the slot empty is answering, not lagging

The in-sync check would override a lock that said the slot held nothing, on the strength of the last PIN it wrote there:

```python
if credential.is_empty:
    # If we recently set a PIN on this slot and it matches the
    # configured PIN, trust the set — the provider may not
    # have caught up yet (eventual consistency, e.g. Schlage cloud API).
    return (self._last_set_pin is not None
            and snapshot.credential_state == self._last_set_pin)
```

The override is right for a lock whose read trails its write. But nothing made it *recent*: `_last_set_pin` is written on every successful set and cleared only by a clear or a restart, so it stood for as long as Home Assistant did. The coordinator compounds it in the wrong direction — a poll that reads the slot empty with no pending write marks the address **verified**, so the `is_verified` guard above passes. A truthful "it's gone" is exactly the input that produced "it's fine."

A Matter credential deleted out of band therefore read as synchronized forever, and got no tick to put it back, because a slot in sync is a slot with nothing to do.

This gives the write the deadline it was already described as having, reusing `PENDING_WRITE_TTL` rather than adding a second number — the seam and the sync layer ask one question about one write, and two answers would drift. The constant moves to `const.py` so both import it without a cycle.

The unreadable branch deliberately keeps no deadline. A write-only lock never stops withholding its contents, so there is no later read for the write to lose a race against; expiring it there would put every Matter slot permanently out of sync and rewrite it on a loop. There is a test pinning that.

## 2. A lock holding a canonical name is not rejecting one for its charset

The Matter userName cascade writes `lcm:<slot>:<name>`, then `lcm<slot>`, then the bare slot number, descending each time the lock refuses. It exists for firmware that restricts `userName` to alphanumerics. It fired on **any** refusal.

Nothing in the exception says which refusal it was. A charset constraint and a momentarily busy lock both arrive as the same catch-all `MatterError`:

```python
UnknownError("InteractionModelError: InvalidCommand (0x85)")   # error_code=0
```

The interaction-model status lives only in the message string. (The typed `InvalidCommand`, `error_code=9`, is a matter-*server API* error — a different namespace entirely.) Classifying on exception type was the first thing I tried, and **this repo's existing tests for this cascade are what showed it could not work** — `test_set_user_update_tolerates_matter_sdk_error` already encoded the real production shape.

So ask the lock instead. If it is holding a canonical name for another slot right now, it accepts the colons, and whatever it just refused was not about them — descending would trade a display name away for nothing. Retry the canonical name and let the moment pass.

That is what #1538 hit: on a lock storing `lcm:1:User A` and `lcm:2:User B`, three further slots were written `lcm3`, `lcm4`, `lcm5` during a spell of poll failures.

Two things worth being explicit about:

- **Nothing was mis-identified.** `parse_tag("lcm3")` still returns slot 3. Only the display name was lost.
- **The cascade was already recoverable.** It always starts from the canonical name, so the next successful write to a degraded slot restores the display. There is a test for that. It is what lets this change only have to *prevent* the degradation rather than also undo it — but it is also why the reporter's names persisted: nothing writes to a slot that is already in sync, so what a moment cost stayed on the lock.

Only the canonical format counts as proof. `parse_tag` also recognizes the compact and slot-only forms, and accepting those would take the cascade's own output as evidence the cascade was unnecessary. There is a mutant for that.

`async_set_user` now reads the user list once and answers both questions from it — which user anchors the slot, and whether colons are proven — rather than paying a second round trip on a link already timing out.

## Testing

`tests/properties/test_in_sync.py::test_active_empty_credential_trusts_recent_set_only` asserted exactly what the code did, bug included — which is how 100% line coverage sailed past a security-relevant defect. It now states the invariant, with freshness as a `@given` axis.

Mutation-tested rather than trusted to coverage:

| Mutant | Result |
|---|---|
| Drop the TTL guard (bug 1) | killed |
| Invert the TTL comparison | killed |
| Never arm the deadline on a set | killed — *survived the first pass; needed a new test* |
| Arm the deadline in the past | killed |
| Expire the unreadable branch too | killed |
| Gate always open (bug 2) | killed |
| Gate always shut | killed |
| Evidence inverted | killed |
| Compact names count as proof | killed |
| No user ever counts as proof | killed |
| `<=` instead of `<` on the deadline | survives — one instant of a monotonic clock |

The "never arm the deadline" survivor was the useful one: nothing asserted that a set arms the window, and had that line been wrong, Schlage would have read out of sync through its whole cloud lag and rewritten the code every tick.

Three existing UPDATE tests had fixtures where the lock stored a canonical name while the test asserted the cascade descends. Under the new rule those are contradictory, so their fixtures now use the compact form — which is what such a lock would actually be holding.

Full suite green (2349 passed), coverage gate held.

## Scope

Two of four symptoms in #1538; this does not close it. The credential/slot mispairing and the cross-lock deletion are still open — see [my analysis on the issue](https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/issues/1538#issuecomment-5497399377) for what has been ruled out by reproduction and what evidence is still needed.

content.text:
Both fixes are on **PR #1539**, and the issue comment is posted.

## What shipped

**`8b91cc36` — false in-sync.** The empty-read override now expires with `PENDING_WRITE_TTL`. The unreadable branch deliberately doesn't expire; expiring it would put every Matter slot permanently out of sync and rewrite it on a loop, so there's a test pinning that.

**`97f06a07` — the degraded names.** You called it right: classifying was a dead end, and the way out was to stop trying.

The lock is holding the answer. If it's storing `lcm:1:User A` right now, it accepts colons — so whatever it just refused wasn't about the charset, and descending a tier trades a display name away for nothing. Retry instead. No error strings, no counters, no new triggers, and it would have prevented the reporter's `lcm3`/`lcm4`/`lcm5` exactly.

Two things I found while building it that changed the shape of the fix:

**The cascade was already self-healing.** I probed it before writing anything:

```
NAMES TRIED ON A SLOT ALREADY HOLDING 'lcm3': ['lcm:3:User C']
```

It always starts from the canonical name, so the next write to a degraded slot restores the display. The names persisted for one reason only — nothing writes to a slot that's already in sync. That meant the fix only had to *prevent* the degradation, not also undo it, which is why no drift-repair plumbing was needed. There's a test pinning the recovery so that stays true.

**Only the canonical form can count as proof.** `parse_tag` happily recognizes `lcm3` too, and accepting that would take the cascade's own output as evidence the cascade was unnecessary — a gate that unlocks itself. The mutant for it kills 3 tests.

## Verification

Ten mutants across both fixes, all killed. Two were worth the trouble:

- **"Never arm the deadline on a set"** survived the first pass — nothing asserted that a set opens the trust window. Had that line been wrong, Schlage would have read out of sync through its entire cloud lag and rewritten the code every tick.
- **"Compact names count as proof"** — the self-unlocking gate above.

The only survivor is `<=` vs `<` on a monotonic deadline: one instant of a clock, no invariant to reach.

Full suite green, 2349 passed, coverage gate held. I also had to realign three existing UPDATE tests whose fixtures had the lock storing a canonical name *while* asserting the cascade descends — contradictory under the new rule, so they now use the compact form, which is what such a lock would actually hold.

## Still open on #1538

The credential/slot mispairing and the cross-lock deletion. The issue comment asks the reporter for debug logs spanning the removal, and names the specific log lines that would settle it — if `no LCM-owned user to release for slot N` or `Setting usercode on ... slot N` names Lock A during a removal of Lock B, that's the smoking gun.

One note on the first fix worth watching in review: a Schlage cloud lag exceeding 60s will now flap out-of-sync and re-write once, where before it stayed quiet. That's the trade you picked, and I think it's the right one — a stale write shouldn't outvote the lock indefinitely — but it's the one user-visible behaviour change here.

I fetched it as a local branch `pr-1539-review` and read it via `git show` — the working tree is back on the original detached HEAD `c53b5815` with the same uncommitted `.entire/.gitignore` change it started with.

The mechanical parts check out: `PENDING_WRITE_TTL` has no dangling importers after the move to `const.py`, `time` is already imported in `sync.py`, `_user_index_for_slot` is a faithful extraction (including the `adopt_untagged=True` default the set path relied on), `async_get_users` returns raw lock-side names so `is_canonical_tagged_name` really can see canonical tags, and the clear path's `_last_set_pin = None` makes the un-reset `_last_set_expires_at` harmless.

Three findings:

- `custom_components/lock_code_manager/providers/matter.py:824` — MEDIUM-HIGH. `colons_proven` treats every `MatterError` as transient, but the cascade's fallbacks also strip the entire user-supplied display portion, not just the colons. `_build_tagged_user_name` measures the 32-limit in characters while matter.py documents it as 32 *bytes* UTF-8, so a non-ASCII display name passes the client check, gets ConstraintError from the lock as a plain `MatterError`, and — on any lock already storing one canonical name — now aborts instead of descending to `lcm3`. The CREATE path never allocates a user_index, so the slot never gets a PIN, permanently.
- `custom_components/lock_code_manager/providers/matter.py:825` — MEDIUM. The abort raises `LockDisconnected` for something the message itself says is a lock-side refusal on a reachable lock. `async_set_user`'s CREATE-path `except MatterError` doesn't catch it, so it reaches the tick's `except LockDisconnected`, which calls `note_connectivity_failure()`. With `BACKOFF_FAILURE_THRESHOLD = 3` and a 2 s tick, ~6 s of a busy lock marks the whole lock unreachable and suspends every slot on it (and a false `lock_offline` repair at 12), while the slot breaker is never charged so the accurate per-slot suspension can't happen. `LockOperationFailed` is the type that matches "the lock answered and refused".
- `custom_components/lock_code_manager/domain/sync.py:493` — LOW-MEDIUM. Each TTL cycle passes back through IN_SYNC, which calls `_slot_breaker.reset()`, so a lock that keeps reporting the slot empty after a successful set is rewritten every 60 s forever and `MAX_SYNC_ATTEMPTS` is never reached — the silent-wrong-state bug is traded for an unbounded, unreported retry loop. The intended out-of-band-deletion case is unaffected (the rewrite sticks).

# Code Review Reception

## Overview

Code review requires technical evaluation, not emotional performance.

**Core principle:** Verify before implementing. Ask before assuming. Technical correctness over social comfort.

## The Response Pattern

```
WHEN receiving code review feedback:

1. READ: Complete feedback without reacting
2. UNDERSTAND: Restate requirement in own words (or ask)
3. VERIFY: Check against codebase reality
4. EVALUATE: Technically sound for THIS codebase?
5. RESPOND: Technical acknowledgment or reasoned pushback
6. IMPLEMENT: One item at a time, test each
```

## Forbidden Responses

**NEVER:**
- "You're absolutely right!" (explicit CLAUDE.md violation)
- "Great point!" / "Excellent feedback!" (performative)
- "Let me implement that now" (before verification)

**INSTEAD:**
- Restate the technical requirement
- Ask clarifying questions
- Push back with technical reasoning if wrong
- Just start working (actions > words)

## Handling Unclear Feedback

```
IF any item is unclear:
  STOP - do not implement anything yet
  ASK for clarification on unclear items

WHY: Items may be related. Partial understanding = wrong implementation.
```

**Example:**
```
your human partner: "Fix 1-6"
You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.

❌ WRONG: Implement 1,2,3,6 now, ask about 4,5 later
✅ RIGHT: "I understand items 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before proceeding."
```

## Source-Specific Handling

### From your human partner
- **Trusted** - implement after understanding
- **Still ask** if scope unclear
- **No performative agreement**
- **Skip to action** or technical acknowledgment

### From External Reviewers
```
BEFORE implementing:
  1. Check: Technically correct for THIS codebase?
  2. Check: Breaks existing functionality?
  3. Check: Reason for current implementation?
  4. Check: Works on all platforms/versions?
  5. Check: Does reviewer understand full context?

IF suggestion seems wrong:
  Push back with technical reasoning

IF can't easily verify:
  Say so: "I can't verify this without [X]. Should I [investigate/ask/proceed]?"

IF conflicts with your human partner's prior decisions:
  Stop and discuss with your human partner first
```

**your human partner's rule:** "External feedback - be skeptical, but check carefully"

## YAGNI Check for "Professional" Features

```
IF reviewer suggests "implementing properly":
  grep codebase for actual usage

  IF unused: "This endpoint isn't called. Remove it (YAGNI)?"
  IF used: Then implement properly
```

**your human partner's rule:** "You and reviewer both report to me. If we don't need this feature, don't add it."

## Implementation Order

```
FOR multi-item feedback:
  1. Clarify anything unclear FIRST
  2. Then implement in this order:
     - Blocking issues (breaks, security)
     - Simple fixes (typos, imports)
     - Complex fixes (refactoring, logic)
  3. Test each fix individually
  4. Verify no regressions
```

## When To Push Back

Push back when:
- Suggestion breaks existing functionality
- Reviewer lacks full context
- Violates YAGNI (unused feature)
- Technically incorrect for this stack
- Legacy/compatibility reasons exist
- Conflicts with your human partner's architectural decisions

**How to push back:**
- Use technical reasoning, not defensiveness
- Ask specific questions
- Reference working tests/code
- Involve your human partner if architectural

**Signal if uncomfortable pushing back out loud:** "Strange things are afoot at the Circle K"

## Acknowledging Correct Feedback

When feedback IS correct:
```
✅ "Fixed. [Brief description of what changed]"
✅ "Good catch - [specific issue]. Fixed in [location]."
✅ [Just fix it and show in the code]

❌ "You're absolutely right!"
❌ "Great point!"
❌ "Thanks for catching that!"
❌ "Thanks for [anything]"
❌ ANY gratitude expression
```

**Why no thanks:** Actions speak. Just fix it. The code itself shows you heard the feedback.

**If you catch yourself about to write "Thanks":** DELETE IT. State the fix instead.

## Gracefully Correcting Your Pushback

If you pushed back and were wrong:
```
✅ "You were right - I checked [X] and it does [Y]. Implementing now."
✅ "Verified this and you're correct. My initial understanding was wrong because [reason]. Fixing."

❌ Long apology
❌ Defending why you pushed back
❌ Over-explaining
```

State the correction factually and move on.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---------|-----|
| Performative agreement | State requirement or just act |
| Blind implementation | Verify against codebase first |
| Batch without testing | One at a time, test each |
| Assuming reviewer is right | Check if breaks things |
| Avoiding pushback | Technical correctness > comfort |
| Partial implementation | Clarify all items first |
| Can't verify, proceed anyway | State limitation, ask for direction |

## Real Examples

**Performative Agreement (Bad):**
```
Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
❌ "You're absolutely right! Let me remove that..."
```

**Technical Verification (Good):**
```
Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
✅ "Checking... build target is 10.15+, this API needs 13+. Need legacy for backward compat. Current impl has wrong bundle ID - fix it or drop pre-13 support?"
```

**YAGNI (Good):**
```
Reviewer: "Implement proper metrics tracking with database, date filters, CSV export"
✅ "Grepped codebase - nothing calls this endpoint. Remove it (YAGNI)? Or is there usage I'm missing?"
```

**Unclear Item (Good):**
```
your human partner: "Fix items 1-6"
You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.
✅ "Understand 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before implementing."
```

## GitHub Thread Replies

When replying to inline review comments on GitHub, reply in the comment thread (`gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pr}/comments/{id}/replies`), not as a top-level PR comment.

## The Bottom Line

**External feedback = suggestions to evaluate, not orders to follow.**

Verify. Question. Then implement.

No performative agreement. Technical rigor always.

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
fix: the evidence rules out the charset, not the length

Review of the previous commit found the gate claiming more than it knew.

The fallback cascade works around two things, not one: each tier drops
more of the name, so it recovers from a lock that rejects the colons AND
from a name the lock has no room for. Proving the lock accepts colons
rules out the first only. A canonical name over the byte budget was
being treated as a transient refusal and retried forever -- and on the
CREATE path that returns without an allocated user_index, so the slot
never got a PIN at all. Before this gate existed it would have descended
to lcm<slot> and worked, with the display name as the price.

Matter counts userName in UTF-8 BYTES while the name is truncated by
CHARACTERS upstream, so the names this strands are the non-ASCII ones:
32 characters of accented text is 36 bytes, passes the truncation, and
comes back refused. Constant renamed to say which unit it is in.

The abort also raised LockDisconnected for a lock that had just answered.
That charges the LOCK breaker, which counts consecutively and takes every
slot on the lock down as unreachable after three -- over something one
slot's name did, while the slot breaker that exists for exactly this
never sees it. sync.py already spells out the distinction at its own
LockOperationFailed handler. Raise that instead.
MSG
git push -q origin fix/1538-matter-multilock && git log --oneline -3
